-claude,

-codex,

-agents,

-project (P is --prefix, default skills). Search them all with `xerj search --prefix skills` xerj autoindex s3:/// [OPTIONS] discover + index objects in a bucket (r2:// too; see OBJECT STORAGE) xerj autoindex map [OPTIONS] print the data map of what is already indexed xerj autoindex map [OPTIONS] preview a folder that is not indexed yet. Same discovery as `xerj autoindex --dry-run`: walk, sniff, infer, print the plan. Nothing is written to an index. With no folder, `map` reads the catalog on --url xerj autoindex remove --prefix

] [--uncataloged] [--yes] list one folder's indices and catalog rows, then delete them. Nothing is deleted without --yes or a terminal y. Another folder under the same prefix is left in place. -* indices that no catalog row names. xerj autoindex status [OPTIONS] resume-journal + index progress view xerj autoindex s3://bucket/prefix --watch [OPTIONS] poll object storage and emit a change feed MAP REPORTS (catalog map only): --html write an offline HTML report (new file only) --md write a Markdown report (new file only) --redact-paths omit file paths and skip reasons from the report OPTIONS: --url ES-compat endpoint (default http://localhost:9200) --api-key Authorization header (or env XERJ_API_KEY) --workers workers for BOTH phases — content hashing/sniffing and indexing (default: every core, reduced if the memory safe zone cannot pay for that many bulk buffers; a value you pass is honoured and only warned about; valid range 1..=1024) --pdf-workers concurrent PDF parser processes (default min(cores,4); max 4, the default reduced further on a machine with little free memory) --pdf-timeout-secs per-PDF parser timeout (default 120; max 3600) --bulk-mb bulk cut size in MB (default 8, max 24) --bulk-timeout-secs bulk HTTP request timeout in seconds (default 300; valid range 1..=3600) --prefix

index prefix (default ax). One prefix is one source folder. The same prefix on a different folder is refused: datasets are keyed ds:: and indices are -*, so finalize overwrites the earlier datasets. Several repositories under one prefix also collapse: each repo indexed on its own has an empty scope and becomes the single dataset -docs. Use one --prefix per folder, or index the parent folder once. A prefix keeps only [a-z0-9] runs joined by single '-', so a trailing '-' or '_' is dropped (the run warns). -* also matches a sibling prefix that starts with -, so pick prefixes that do not start one another --replace-prefix retire datasets already stored under --prefix that were indexed from a different folder. Prints those folders and continues. Without this flag that run is refused and nothing is written. --dry-run does not bypass it --state-dir resume journal location (default ~/.xerj/autoindex//). On `autoindex remove`, also deletes journal.ndjson in this directory after the folder's indices are removed; the default journal is deleted either way. for an s3:// source this is also where the local object mirror lives, so point it at a disk with room --endpoint-url S3-compatible endpoint for an s3:// source (MinIO, Ceph, R2, localstack). Defaults to $AWS_ENDPOINT_URL_S3, then $AWS_ENDPOINT_URL. Refused for a folder rather than ignored --snapshot-max-gb logical payload cap for sealed source+prepared records bytes (default 64); excludes filesystem/manifest overhead --fresh ignore an existing resume journal and restart, rebuild the plan in place (ids stay idempotent for unchanged bytes). A file republished under a new content key drops the documents previously published for that path. It removes documents for a file that disappeared. It is refused on a durable corpus generation — see RESUME POLICY --follow-symlinks follow symlinks (loop-safe); off by default. A link is judged by what it RESOLVES to: a target outside the folder is refused, and one inside a hidden directory is skipped like any dotfile, whatever the link itself is called --follow-symlinks-outside-root also follow links that resolve OUTSIDE the folder. Requires --follow-symlinks. Off by default; pointing at a folder is not consent to index whatever it links to. The hidden-file rule still applies to the target, judged from where it diverges from your folder — so a dotted directory the two paths SHARE does not refuse anything, because your folder is already inside it --stub index matching files as ONE existence-only name card (title + provenance); contents are never opened. Repeatable. A pattern without '/' matches file names anywhere ('*.bvh'); with '/' it matches the root-relative path ('unity/**/*.csv'). '**' crosses directories --exclude leave matching paths out of the index entirely (not \ walked, not counted). Repeatable, same glob syntax \ as --stub ('gen/**', '*.log'). Use it for a tree you do \ not want to edit an ignore file for. \ --no-ignore index everything: no .gitignore, no .xerjignore, no .git/info/exclude, no built-in defaults. Hidden files (.env, .git/, .ssh) stay skipped either way — that is not an ignore rule, it is what keeps secrets out. --no-default-ignores keep the ignore files, drop only the built-in list (node_modules/ bower_components/ vendor/ third_party/ thirdparty/ target/ dist/ build/ .venv/ __pycache__/ *.png *.jpg *.jpeg *.gif *.webp *.ico *.bmp *.woff *.woff2 *.ttf *.otf *.wasm *.so *.dll *.dylib *.exe) --max-file-gb skip+record oversized non-streamable files, cap in whole GB (default 2). Use --max-file-mb/--max-file-bytes for a smaller cap; the three are mutually exclusive --max-file-mb same cap expressed in whole MB (e.g. 10 for a source watcher); mutually exclusive with --max-file-gb/-bytes --max-file-bytes same cap expressed in whole bytes; mutually exclusive with --max-file-gb/--max-file-mb AST source files have a separate fixed 2 MiB code cap (2097152 bytes); these flags do not raise it. Oversized source is skipped with a size reason, including hand-written code. --sample records sampled per file for inference (default 500) --no-semantic skip semantic_text on body fields (pure BM25+keyword) --code-analyzer standard (default) or code: `code` declares the built-in identifier-aware analyzer (splits snake_case/camelCase, keeps the original token) on NEWLY created datasets holding source code; existing indexes keep theirs. Measured +0.11 file-localization acc@5 (#1198); costs ~15% index size and ~2.4x text-analysis time --brain second-brain name; relationship edges land in .xerj-memory--edges (default: folder name slug) --no-graph skip relationship detection (wikilinks, local links, section order, directory chains) — no edges are written --watch index once, then stay resident and reindex what changes. Needs --no-graph. A graph-path rerun sweeps a deleted file (exit 3, files-removed) and indexes an added file that fits a frozen dataset. A file that needs a new dataset still stops (exit 3, stale-resume-plan) until --fresh. One OS watch per indexed directory, no polling; respects the same ignore rules as a re-run. docs/LIVE_REINDEXING.md has the measurements. It watches the working tree and never fetches a git remote: it reindexes what a `git pull` changes, and without --watch you re-run the same command. --debounce --watch quiet period before a pass (default 400, max 60000). One editor save is several filesystem events. --max-minutes stop and ask before indexing if phase A's MEASURED estimate is longer than this (default 10; 0 disables the gate; max 10080). See ESTIMATE + DECISION GATE below. --approve answer a decision request: proceed | fast | cancel. `fast` also applies --no-semantic --no-graph. `narrower` is NOT accepted here — it means re-running against a subdirectory, which this flag cannot do. --yes, -y alias for --approve proceed. When the default index plan does not fit the disk budget, --yes takes the recommended plan that does fit. It does not index a plan that is over budget. It does not delete indexed files a smaller plan leaves out; that is --drop-indexed. On `autoindex remove` it is the confirmation: without it a non-terminal run prints the plan and exits 4. It does not choose a folder. --root

(`autoindex remove`) the one folder to drop when --prefix holds more than one. Refused on any other command --max-index-size cap the estimated index (bytes, or a KB/MB/GB suffix). The disk budget is the free space under the node's flood-stage watermark; this flag lowers that cap. 0 is rejected --plan index with one plan: default, skip-vendored, skip-data, code-and-docs, no-vectors, cap-1mb, code-and-docs-no-vectors. A named plan runs even when the estimate says it does not fit (warned). See DISK BUDGET. --drop-indexed delete already-indexed files a reduced plan leaves out. Without this flag that re-run exits 4 and lists them. --plan and --yes do not agree to the deletion. --dry-run walk+sniff+infer, print the plan, index nothing. `autoindex map ` is this same preview --walk-only stop after the walk. Prints each top-level folder's file count and size, what the ignore rules would drop and which rule, and the totals. Stops before hashing: no digest, no sniff, nothing indexed. Ignore files are still read, as on every walk. The node is still contacted, as with --dry-run. --dry-run itself still hashes, sniffs and prints the plan --label label each document at ingest through POST /_decide (#1062): the question-set file's noul/choice questions are rendered against each record's fields and the vote stamped on as label + label_p (and label_ + label__p per question). p is the RAW decide confidence - calibration is #1063. One /_decide call per noul (per option, for a choice) per document. --json machine-readable RESULT on stdout (map: raw catalog docs). Orthogonal to --progress, which owns stderr. --progress liveness on stderr: auto|plain|json|none (default auto). auto = live redrawn line when stderr is a terminal, otherwise one parseable line per interval. plain and json force that shape everywhere (CI, pipes, agents). --progress-interval progress cadence, 1..=3600 (default 1 on a terminal, 5 otherwise). This is the guaranteed upper bound on silence between phases. --quiet errors only (implies --progress none). The decision gate NEVER prompts under this flag, even at a terminal — the question would be silenced with everything else. It emits the JSON decision request on stdout and exits 4 instead, exactly like an agent-driven run. See ESTIMATE + DECISION GATE. --dataset (map, no folder) show one autoindex dataset (not a managed corpus slug) --offset (map, no folder) skip the first N dataset detail sections --limit (map, no folder) how many dataset detail sections to print (default: all of them when there are few, otherwise the first page — the summary table always lists every dataset) --disable-feedback do not print the feedback invitation above; honoured in any position, including after --help (env XERJ_DISABLE_FEEDBACK=true) --help, -h this help IGNORE RULES: The fastest file is the one that is never read, so junk is dropped during the walk, not after it. Honoured, highest precedence first: .xerjignore same syntax as .gitignore, XERJ-only. Use it to exclude something git tracks, or to re-include (!pattern) something git ignores. Outranks .gitignore at any depth. !pattern cannot re-include a hidden (dot-named) entry: see HIDDEN below. .gitignore including nested ones and negation; the closest file wins. .git/info/exclude per-checkout excludes, including nested checkouts. built-in node_modules/ bower_components/ vendor/ third_party/ thirdparty/ target/ dist/ build/ .venv/ __pycache__/ *.png *.jpg *.jpeg *.gif *.webp *.ico *.bmp *.woff *.woff2 *.ttf *.otf *.wasm *.so *.dll *.dylib *.exe Both git-owned kinds stop at a repository boundary, exactly as git does: a .gitignore above a nested checkout does not judge files inside it, so vendored and submoduled trees keep their own rules. .xerjignore and the built-in list are XERJ's, not git's, and apply throughout the folder. Your global gitignore (core.excludesFile) is NOT read: a machine-wide preference should not silently decide what is in your index. A directory the rules reject is never descended, so nothing inside it is stat-ed, hashed or sent. Every run prints what was dropped and by which rule; --dry-run and --walk-only additionally count the non-hidden files inside each pruned directory (bounded — past the budget the count is reported as `at least N`, and xerj-done carries ignored_files_in_pruned_dirs_exact=false to say so). The folder you name is never rejected: if it is itself ignored, it is indexed anyway and the run says which rule it would have matched. HIDDEN: dot-named files and directories below the folder (.env, .git, .ssh, ./) are skipped by a separate rule that runs before any ignore file. No .xerjignore !pattern and no --no-ignore lifts it (the run warns when a .xerjignore tries). To index one, name it as the root, which is never rejected: xerj autoindex ./.openfox --prefix openfox OBJECT STORAGE: `xerj autoindex s3://bucket/prefix` indexes objects instead of files. `r2://bucket/prefix` is the same thing and needs --endpoint-url with the account host. Credentials come from AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID / AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY (+ AWS_SESSION_TOKEN) in the ENVIRONMENT ONLY — no profile files, no instance metadata, no SSO — and never from the URL. A non-empty prefix is treated as a FOLDER: s3://b/docs lists docs/ and not docs-old/. The effective prefix is printed at the start of the run. CHANGE DETECTION is the object's ETag plus its size, recorded in /object-source.json. The ETag is treated as an opaque token, so a multipart upload's `-N` form is fine and nothing is compared to an MD5. A re-run downloads only what changed; an unchanged prefix downloads nothing. THE BYTES ARE MIRRORED to /object-cache// and the ordinary walk runs over that mirror, so extraction sees exactly the bytes it sees for a folder. Budget local disk for the prefix you index. The INDEX still lives on the XERJ node at --url; nothing is written to the bucket. Objects whose keys cannot be a safe local path are skipped and named: `..`, an empty component, a backslash, a control character, a trailing dot or space, a Windows reserved name, and any dot-prefixed component (so a bucket's .env and .git/ stay out of the index, exactly as in a folder). COST: one run costs ceil(objects/1000) class-A LIST requests plus one class-B GET per changed object, and never writes. Counts are BILLED WIRE ATTEMPTS: a request the store throttled and the client retried counts once per attempt, because that is what the store bills. Every run prints what it spent and what running it hourly or every 5 minutes would spend against a 1,000,000/month class-A allowance — read that line before adding a cron. A run that fails mid-transfer records the objects it already fetched, so a re-run pays for the rest only — but it re-lists, so the LIST cost recurs. PDF EXTRACTION: Each PDF uses a fresh process. Limits: 512 MiB input, 32 MiB worker output, 100,000 pages, and a 1.5 GiB address-space cap on Unix where the OS accepts RLIMIT_AS. If the OS refuses that cap (EINVAL or EPERM, as on macOS 27), the refusal is logged once and the worker still starts. The cap is crash isolation, not a security sandbox; non-Unix platforms have no OS memory cap. Image-only pages need OCR. Page parse failures reject the whole PDF instead of silently creating a partial index. XERJ_PDF_WORKER_BIN is a trusted, developer-only executable override. On Linux, fresh runs attempt to retain each validated PDF extraction in bounded anonymous storage under --state-dir. Live admission-time checks attempt to preserve disk and descriptor headroom; refused artifacts are parsed again in phase B and reported under pdf_extraction_reuse. Other platforms currently disable this optimization. Frozen-plan resumes skip phase A and parse unfinished PDFs once. --pdf-workers bounds both phase-A parser processes and phase-B replay materialization; --workers does not widen that PDF memory gate. INCREMENTAL RECONCILIATION: Generated journals with --no-graph reconcile added, removed, moved, and changed files. Graph-enabled journals absorb an added file that fits a frozen dataset, delete documents for a file that disappeared, and leave a file that needs a new dataset unindexed until --fresh rebuilds the plan. Each changed generation currently copies and prepares the full corpus (O(N)); the latest full snapshot remains retained, and cleanup re-reads protected artifacts to verify them. --snapshot-max-gb limits logical staged payload bytes before each write; it is not a physical disk-space or peak-allocation guarantee. EMBEDDINGS: autoindex sends semantic_text to the running server; it does not choose the server's embedding backend. The default is lexical (not neural). For the experimental ONNX backend, start xerj with `--embed-mode onnx-experimental --onnx-model MODEL.onnx --onnx-tokenizer tokenizer.json`, then run autoindex. ONNX runs only for fields inferred as semantic_text (normally long body text; short/structured datasets may infer none). Use --dry-run or `autoindex map` to confirm a semantic field before attributing an indexing result to embeddings. PROGRESS STREAM: stdout is the RESULT, stderr is PROGRESS — pipe them separately. Every run that reaches an exit — success OR error — ends with one terminal line, in every progress mode EXCEPT `none` (which --quiet selects), so an outcome never has to be guessed from silence: xerj-done ok=true exit=3 reason=completed-with-junk wall=57.6s … The terminal line also carries code coverage — code_files=N code_files_indexed=M code_files_junked=K — so a corpus whose source files were ALL dropped cannot print the same line as a healthy one. code_files>0 with code_files_indexed=0 is always a defect, and the run says so in words as well. --quiet/--progress none prints no progress and NO terminal line (only a fatal `error:` line, if any) — poll `autoindex status --state-dir ` or read the exit code instead of waiting for output that never comes. (A run killed by a signal cannot print one either; a missing terminal line after the process is gone means it died, not that it finished.) --progress plain writes TWO lines per tick, in one write: xerj-bar [######################--] 93.4% | index | 8082/8083 items | eta 7s xerj-progress phase=index basis=bytes pct=93.4 items=8082/8083 eta_s=7.2 … `xerj-bar` is the DISPLAY line — self-contained, meant to be shown to a person verbatim by whatever is relaying the run. It is spaced at most one per 15s, plus one per phase change and never two closer than 2s, so it does not flood a transcript. Short phases therefore draw fewer bars than transitions — read the machine line for those. `xerj-progress` is the MACHINE line and keeps the --progress-interval cadence; parse that one. --progress json stays one object per line and carries the same rendered string in a `bar` field on the same schedule: a string on the ticks that owe a bar, null in between. Every record is identified by its leading token, and that is enforced: paths and other outside text are stripped of control characters and bounded before they reach any line, so a crafted filename cannot forge a record or repaint your terminal. `pct`/`eta_s` are the literal word `unknown` (JSON null) whenever they cannot be computed honestly, never a filler number — and the drawn bar obeys the same rule: `[????…]` when there is no denominator, and a full bar only at a real 100%. PHASES, in order. Every long step is a phase of its own, so a line that still says `scan` at 100% means scan — not indexing: default (graph) path: walk, hash, scan, prepare, graph, index, graph-corpus, finalize-refresh (one refresh per dataset, the in-flight index named), finalize-count, finalize-correlate, finalize-histogram, finalize-catalog --no-graph path: walk, hash, scan, prepare (install mappings), snapshot (seal + extract, bytes), index (sealed bulk bytes, the in-flight file named), finalize-catalog, finalize-refresh (one refresh per dataset), finalize-verify (read-backs batched into per-index digest windows, one search per window). A resumed run starts at `replay` and its `index` phase counts only the operations still to apply. ESTIMATE + DECISION GATE: Phase A already reads and parses every file to sniff and sample it, so it measures throughput per format family ON THIS MACHINE. autoindex turns that into a RANGE (never one confident number) for the indexing phase and prints the basis with it. Families phase A never read end to end are named and left OUT of the arithmetic instead of being priced at some other family's rate; if nothing could be measured, it says so and does not gate. The range covers CLIENT-SIDE EXTRACTION only — server indexing, embedding and network time are not in it, which is why the gate compares the upper end. If that upper end is longer than --max-minutes and no --approve/--yes was given, nothing is indexed: a JSON decision request goes to stdout and the process exits 4 (a code of its own — 1 is the catch-all for real failures). Answer by re-running the same command with --approve proceed|fast|cancel. A person at a terminal is prompted instead — but ONLY when the question can actually be seen. All three must hold: stdin is a terminal, stderr is a terminal, and the progress surface is on. --quiet / --progress none silences the question, so those runs are never prompted and never wait on stdin; a piped or agent-driven run is not prompted either. Every un-prompted run behaves identically: the JSON decision request goes to stdout (which --quiet does NOT silence) and the process exits 4. The payload's `prompt_not_offered_because` says which of the three was missing. autoindex never waits on stdin for a question it did not print. WORK ORDER: Phase B drains source and documents first, then configuration, then structured data, then logs and line files, and vendored/generated/minified paths last — so stopping early, or searching while it runs, still gives you the files you cared about. Inside a band the biggest file starts first (with several workers it then runs alongside the rest instead of becoming the tail); a single-worker run goes smallest-first instead. One exception: a file so large that it outlasts everything ranked above it starts first whatever band it is in. The full breakdown is printed with the plan. RESUME POLICY: generated --no-graph journals reconcile add, change, delete, rename, and no-op runs; a --no-graph state directory written before the generation format must be rebuilt into a new --state-dir and --prefix; graph-enabled journals reconcile added files that fit a frozen dataset, delete documents for files that disappeared, and keep crash-resume of an interrupted run. On a graph-enabled journal, unchanged runs and same-path replacements reuse the durable plan. Added files that fit a frozen dataset are indexed; files needing a new dataset report exit 3, stale-resume-plan and ok=false. Use --fresh to rebuild that graph plan and include them. Removed files are swept with reason=files-removed. A wider exclusion rule requires --drop-indexed approval before its previously indexed documents are swept. --fresh is not a destination wipe. It is refused once a durable corpus generation exists: rerun without it to reconcile changes incrementally. A pre-generation --no-graph journal needs an isolated rebuild under a new --state-dir and --prefix. For any independent graph rebuild also use a new --brain (or --no-graph). Validate before switching readers; explicitly clean the shared autoindex-catalog and old target only after validation. WATCH (OBJECT STORAGE): `xerj autoindex s3:/// --watch` polls the bucket with ListObjectsV2 and emits one JSON event per changed object (added / changed / deleted) on stdout, or to --events-out. It does NOT index: pipe the feed into the indexer. Deletes are detected only by a full scan (not --append-only). A bucket has no inotify, so this is polling, and polling costs money: ListObjectsV2 is a CLASS A operation, one call per page (--page-size keys, 1,000 by default and at most), EVERY cycle, whether anything changed or not. Cloudflare R2's free tier is 1,000,000 Class A operations a month, which is ~23 per minute for the whole account: objects list calls/cycle every 60s every 300s (default) 1,000 1 43,200/mo 8,640/mo 10,000 10 432,000/mo 86,400/mo 100,000 100 4,320,000/mo 864,000/mo 1,000,000 1,000 43,200,000/mo 8,640,000/mo The default interval is 300s and the default budget is 200000 Class A and 2000000 Class B operations a month (20% of each free tier, because the rest of the account spends from it too). The budget is a CIRCUIT BREAKER, checked on every cycle: a projection over budget (also when the bucket grows mid-watch), or a month whose budget is spent (counted across restarts in /objwatch-spend.json), STOPS the watch with exit 4 and a decision request. --allow-cost accepts the spend, --append-only makes a growing key space cost one call per cycle, and a narrower prefix is free. --poll-interval seconds between cycles (default 300, max 86400) --once / --max-cycles N stop after one / N cycles --no-fetch metadata-only: compare ETag+size+mtime, never GET --append-only list only keys above the highest one seen (start-after): one list call per cycle, and NO delete or older-key change detection — opt in only for an append-only key space such as date-partitioned logs --dry-run one cycle, no GETs, nothing emitted, no journal: price the poll. The listing itself is real and IS billed (ceil(keys/page-size) Class A ops, on the ledger) --endpoint-url S3 endpoint (else AWS_ENDPOINT_URL). R2: https://.r2.cloudflarestorage.com --region signing region (else AWS_REGION, else auto) --max-object-mb byte cap per fetched object (default 64) --max-monthly-ops Class A budget per month (default 200000) --max-monthly-gets Class B (GET) budget per month (default 2000000) --allow-cost proceed although the projection is over budget --page-size keys per list call (default 1000, the API maximum) --events-out write the JSONL change feed here instead of stdout --status-file running counts an operator can read (default /objwatch-status.json) Credentials come from the environment only: AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID, AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY, optionally AWS_SESSION_TOKEN. Never from a flag. DISK BUDGET: Before hashing, autoindex counts files by extension (code, prose, pdf, data, binary, other) and by top-level folder, and estimates the index from measured per-kind ratios. The budget is the free space on the node's data volume under the flood-stage watermark (the same GET /_cat/allocation read that refuses a volume already at the watermark), optionally lowered with --max-index-size. A node that does not report disk.flood_stage is not guessed at. When the default plan fits, the run continues. When it does not, stdout carries a JSON plan list and the run exits 4 unless --yes takes the recommended plan that fits, or --plan names one (a named plan is the override: it runs over the estimate with a warning; the estimate errs high). A reduced plan on a folder that is already indexed does not delete the files it leaves out. That re-run exits 4 and lists the files and the datasets a reconcile would remove, until --drop-indexed confirms it. --yes chooses a plan; it does not agree to delete indexed data. A terminal with the question visible is asked. Kinds without a calibration are reported as unmeasured and do not refuse the run. Skipped files are listed after the ok: line (up to 20, then a count). A folder already indexed under another prefix is named before the walk. EXIT CODES: 0 complete (also: gate answered with --approve cancel); 3 completed-with-junk (junk recorded, never fatal) — SUCCESS: the index is searchable, and the summary on stdout opens with a line starting `ok:` that says so (xerj-done carries ok=true), except stale-resume-plan below. Treat 0 and 3 alike as a finished run. This includes a dataset whose mapping the server REFUSED: its files are recorded as junk with the server's reason, the xerj-done line carries datasets_refused / files_refused, and every other dataset is indexed; or catalog-alias-sweep-failed — the corpus IS indexed and the journal committed; only the catalog's duplicate-alias cleanup could not run. Read `reason` on the xerj-done line to tell the two apart, and rerun the same command once the reported server condition clears; or stale-resume-plan — files on disk appeared after the resume plan was frozen. They are not counted as junk. `skipped_appeared` is the count; the summary names the first few paths and says to re-run with --fresh to rebuild the plan in place and include them. For this exit 3, the xerj-done line carries ok=false and the summary opens with `not ok:`, because the files it skipped are not searchable. Read `reason` to tell this apart from completed-with-junk; or files-removed — a graph-path rerun deleted documents, catalog rows and edges for files that left the folder. The index matches the folder; the next unchanged rerun is exit 0. Read `reason` to tell this apart from completed-with-junk; 4 NEEDS A DECISION — the estimate exceeded --max-minutes, the estimated index does not fit the disk budget, a reduced plan would delete files that are already indexed, or a --watch poll cost more than --max-monthly-ops; nothing was indexed and a JSON decision request is on stdout. A plan that does not fit is not started, including with --yes. Already-indexed files are not deleted unless --drop-indexed is also set; 2 usage; 1 runtime failure, including endpoint/journal failure, a refused removal or unsafe state transition, verification failure, or pdf-worker-unavailable (the isolated PDF parser could not start). Files may already be indexed. Read `reason` on the xerj-done line; the summary on stdout opens with `not ok:`
